anf_compare.notes: No ANF/NPNF English of this work; translated from the PG 74 Greek only.

bible_refs.note: Lemma quoted verbatim (τὸν μὴ γνόντα ἁμαρτίαν ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν ἁμαρτίαν ἐποίησεν ἵνα ἡμεῖς γενώμεθα δικαιοσύνη θεοῦ ἐν αὐτῷ) and its purpose clause repeated later with ὁ μὴ εἰδὼς ἁμαρτίαν.
ὑπέμεινε σταυρὸν αἰσχύνης καταφρονήσας, quoted (marked in the source).
εἷς ὑπὲρ πάντων ἀπέθανεν matches 2 Corinthians 5:14; ὁ πάντων ἀντάξιος is Cyril's addition, not cited.

LXX Hosea 4:8 (ἁμαρτίας λαοῦ μου φάγονται καὶ ἐν ταῖς ἀδικίαις αὐτῶν λήμψονται τὰς ψυχὰς αὐτῶν); the Hebrew-based English reads differently ('they feed on the sin of my people; they set their heart on their iniquity'). Translated as Cyril quotes the LXX.
οὐκ ἐξ ἔργων τῶν ἐν δικαιοσύνῃ ὧν ἐποιήσαμεν ἡμεῖς, ἀλλὰ κατὰ τὸ πολὺ αὐτοῦ ἔλεος: Titus 3:5 has ἃ for ὧν and τὸ αὐτοῦ ἔλεος without πολύ; Cyril applies it to justification.
New lemma Αὐτὸς δὲ ἐγὼ Παῦλος παρακαλῶ ὑμᾶς διὰ τῆς πραότητος καὶ ἐπιεικείας τοῦ Χριστοῦ κ.τ.λ.; 'and so on' renders κ.τ.λ.
μωρίαν ἡγοῦντο τὸν τοῦ Σωτῆρος σταυρόν echoes 1 Corinthians 1:23 (Ἕλλησιν δὲ μωρίαν), applied to Athenian sages.
σπερμολόγος is the Athenians' word for Paul in Acts 17:18.
δοῦλον Κυρίου οὐ δεῖ μάχεσθαι ἀλλ' ἤπιον εἶναι πρὸς πάντας … ἐν πραότητι παιδεύοντα τοὺς ἀντιδιατιθεμένους; Cyril omits διδακτικόν, ἀνεξίκακον between the clauses. Only what he quotes is translated.
Ἐμοὶ γὰρ τὸ ζῆν Χριστὸς καὶ τὸ ἀποθανεῖν κέρδος verbatim.
ὃς λοιδορούμενος οὐκ ἀντελοιδόρει, πάσχων οὐκ ἠπείλει, παρεδίδου δὲ τῷ κρίνοντι δικαίως verbatim; παρεδίδου has no object in Greek, and 'entrusted Himself' follows the usual English sense.

Cyril's expanded paraphrase (adds οὐ γαῦρος, οὔτε μὴν ἠκονημένος εἰς ἔριδάς τε καὶ μάχας; δέομαι δὲ καὶ νῦν μὴ παρὼν θαῤῥῆσαι follows 10:2 δέομαι δὲ τὸ μὴ παρὼν θαρρῆσαι). Not in quotation marks because it is paraphrase.
ὅπου γὰρ ζῆλος καὶ ἔρις ἐν ὑμῖν, οὐχὶ σαρκικοί ἐστε καὶ κατὰ ἄνθρωπον περιπατεῖτε; (word order slightly changed).

choices.english: he says of the God and Father: 'Him who knew no sin He made sin'
choices.why: Agency kept exact: the Father is the subject of 'made sin'; capitalised pronouns keep the Father, Christ and Paul apart.

choices.english: they called the victims slain for sin 'sins'
choices.why: LXX usage of ἁμαρτία for the sin offering; translated as Cyril states it.

choices.why: Negation kept: the Word, being God, cannot sin.
rejected: did not know he did wrong

choices.why: Crucifixion between criminals; perfect rendered as a simple English past with the result implied.

choices.term: δέομαι δὲ καὶ νῦν μὴ παρὼν θαῤῥῆσαι

choices.why: Negation and modality of 2 Corinthians 10:2 kept exact.
rejected: I ask now to be bold when present

pass_a_gloss: [opens mid-sentence; prior row ends '…and toward persuading them easily not to'] fall back into slackness, but rather to lay hold of the life in Christ; and he says about the God and Father: 'Him not having known sin on our behalf he made sin, so that we might become righteousness of God in him.' Like as if he were saying: The one having sinned nothing ever he arranged to suffer the [lot] of those exceedingly sin-loving, so that he might show us righteous, having received faith into him; for he endured 'the cross, despising shame'; for one on behalf of all died, the one worth-equal to all. When therefore he is said to become sin, do not suppose that he has committed sin; for the Word, being God, does not know how to offend; but know rather that he has been given by the God and Father for our sins; just as indeed also the victims for sin, according to the law of Moses, they named 'sins'; it is written at least in prophets about those ordered to act as priests [page 356]: 'Sins of my people they will eat, and in their iniquities they will take their souls'; for they ate the sacrifices for sins according to the law, the overseers and ministers of the divine altars. Great therefore toward shame for those wishing to be slack [is] to ponder wisely that he was condemned together with the sinners and has been hung together for us, the one not knowing sin, so that we might become righteousness of God in him; for we have been justified by the God and Father 'not out of works in righteousness which we did, but according to his great mercy' through faith in Christ. 'I myself Paul exhort you through the meekness and gentleness of Christ, etc.' Many were of the wise at Athens, living together with those in Corinth, who considered the cross of the Savior foolishness, and the one announcing the word of the God-inspired scripture, a charlatan and seed-picker/babbler, together with the other saints, they named also the blessed Paul himself; and certain others of those from circumcision clung upon/attacked again the believers, praising circumcision and the legal sacrifices, and saying the blessed Paul to be beside himself, as having chosen impiously to war against the ancient decrees. Against such [men] the zealous of the Corinthians were spurred on, and very fittingly, and wanted to bring hands upon them as enemies of the divine preaching; but since the matter was very unseemly, and as far as possible from the gentleness befitting saints — 'for a slave of the Lord must not fight, according to what is written, but be gentle [page 357] toward all, in meekness instructing the opponents' — he commands, saying: I myself Paul, the sacred-minister of the divine mysteries, the steward and apostle, the one conspicuous in zeal, whetting you yourselves too to say with me 'For to me to live is Christ and to die gain', exhort you through the meekness and gentleness of Christ, 'who being reviled did not revile back, suffering did not threaten, but handed over to the one judging justly.' Opportunely therefore he brings them into remembrance of the life of Christ, setting [them] most meek and gentle; and I myself, he says, Paul, who when present among you face to face am lowly, not haughty, nor indeed sharpened for strifes and fights, who am bold while absent, and I ask even now not, being present, to be bold; because, as it comes upon me to reckon, in no way will you dare against certain [people] supposing us to walk as according to flesh, that is, to conduct life fleshly in strife and zeal/jealousy; 'for where,' he says, 'jealousy and strife [are] among you, are you not fleshly and walk according to man?' Better therefore than their suspicion it befits to become those wishing to follow the gentlenesses of the Savior, and not to walk fleshly. For if some disobey, it is not necessary, beating them down with clubs, to force them, but rather to wait for the willing [cut off; continues in u04-rem-close with 'turning of theirs toward God'].
pass_b_english: … fall back into carelessness, but rather to take firm hold of the life that is in Christ. And he says of the God and Father: “Him who knew no sin He made sin for us, so that we might become the righteousness of God in Him” (2 Corinthians 5:21). It is as if he were saying: He caused the One who had never sinned at all to suffer the lot of those who greatly love sin, so that He might show us, who have received faith in Him, to be righteous. For He endured “the cross, despising the shame” (Hebrews 12:2); for One died for all (2 Corinthians 5:14), He whose worth equals that of all.

So when He is said to have become sin, do not suppose that He committed sin; for the Word, being God, does not know how to do wrong. Know rather that He was given by the God and Father for our sins, just as, under the law of Moses, they called the victims slain for sin “sins.” At any rate it is written in the prophets about those appointed to serve as priests: “They will eat the sins of My people, and in their iniquities they will take their souls” (Hosea 4:8). For under the law the overseers and ministers of the divine altars ate the sacrifices offered for sins.

It is a great means, then, of shaming those who would be careless, to ponder wisely that He who did not know sin was condemned with sinners and hung beside them for our sake, so that we might become the righteousness of God in Him (2 Corinthians 5:21). For we have been justified by the God and Father “not by works of righteousness that we have done, but according to His great mercy” (Titus 3:5), through faith in Christ.
“I, Paul, myself entreat you by the meekness and gentleness of Christ,” and so on (2 Corinthians 10:1).

Many of the wise men of Athens lived among the people of Corinth. They regarded the Savior’s cross as foolishness (1 Corinthians 1:23), and they called the blessed Paul himself, the herald of the word of inspired Scripture, a charlatan and a babbler (Acts 17:18), together with the other saints. Some others of the circumcision, in turn, were setting upon the believers, praising circumcision and the sacrifices of the law, and saying that the blessed Paul was out of his mind, as one who had impiously chosen to make war on the ancient decrees. Against such men the zealous among the Corinthians were stirred up, and quite naturally; they wanted to lay hands on them as enemies of the divine preaching.

But the thing was most unseemly, and as far as could be from the gentleness that befits saints; for, as it is written, “the Lord’s servant must not quarrel, but be kind to all, correcting his opponents with meekness” (2 Timothy 2:24–25). So he gives them a charge, saying: I, Paul myself, the priest of the divine mysteries, the steward and apostle, the one renowned for zeal, who spur you yourselves on to say with me, “For to me to live is Christ, and to die is gain” (Philippians 1:21), entreat you by the meekness and gentleness of Christ, “who when He was reviled did not revile in return, when He suffered did not threaten, but entrusted Himself to Him who judges justly” (1 Peter 2:23). So at the right moment he brings them to remember the life of Christ, and makes them most meek and gentle.

I, Paul myself, he says, who am lowly when present among you face to face, not haughty, nor sharpened for quarrels and fights; who am bold when absent, I ask even now that when present I may not have to be bold (2 Corinthians 10:1–2). For, as I am minded to think, you will by no means take bold action against certain people who think that we walk, as it were, according to the flesh, that is, live in a fleshly way, in strife and jealousy. For, he says, “where there is jealousy and strife among you, are you not fleshly, and walking in a human way?” (1 Corinthians 3:3).

Those, then, who wish to follow the Savior’s gentleness ought to rise above the suspicion of those men and not walk in a fleshly way. For if some disobey, one must not beat them down with clubs and force them, but rather wait for their willing …

ἀναπίπτειν εἰς ῥᾳθυμίας, ἐπιδράξασθαι δὲ μᾶλλον τῆς ἐν Χριστῷ ζωῆς· καί φησι περὶ
τοῦ Θεοῦ καὶ Πατρός Τὸν μὴ γνόντα ἁμαρτίαν ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν ἁμαρτίαν ἐποίησεν ἵνα ἡμεῖς
γενώμεθα δικαιοσύνη Θεοῦ ἐν αὐτῷ. ὅμοιον ὡσεὶ λέγοι Τὸν οὐδὲν ἡμαρτηκότα πώποτε
παρεσκεύασε παθεῖν τὸ τῶν σφόδρα φιλαμαρτημόνων, ἵν' ἡμᾶς ἀποφήνῃ δικαίους τὴν
εἰς αὐτὸν πίστιν εἰσδεδεγμένους· ὑπέμεινε γὰρ "σταυρὸν, "αἰσχύνης καταφρονήσας·" εἷς
γὰρ ὑπὲρ πάντων ἀπέθανεν ὁ πάντων ἀντάξιος. ὅταν τοίνυν ἁμαρτία γενέσθαι λέγηται,
μὴ ὑπολάβῃς ὅτι πέπραχεν ἁμαρτίαν· οὐ γὰρ οἶδεν πλημμελεῖν Θεὸς ὢν ὁ Λόγος· ἴσθι δὲ
μᾶλλον ὅτι δέδοται παρὰ τοῦ Θεοῦ καὶ Πατρὸς ὑπὲρ τῶν ἁμαρτιῶν ἡμῶν· καθάπερ
ἀμέλει καὶ τὰ ὑπὲρ ἁμαρτίας σφάγια, κατὰ τὸν Μωσέως νόμον, ἁμαρτίας ὠνόμαζον·
γέγραπται γοῦν ἐν προφήταις περὶ τῶν 356 ἱερᾶσθαι προστεταγμένων "Ἁμαρτίας λαοῦ
μου φάγονται, "καὶ ἐν ταῖς ἀδικίαις αὐτῶν λήψονται τὰς ψυχὰς αὐτῶν·" ἤσθιον γὰρ τὰ
ὑπὲρ ἁμαρτιῶν θύματα κατὰ τὸν νόμον, οἱ τῶν θείων θυσιαστηρίων ἐπιμεληταὶ καὶ
διάκονοι. μέγα τοίνυν πρὸς ἐντροπὴν τοῖς ἐθέλουσι ῥᾳθυμεῖν τὸ διενθυμεῖσθαι σοφῶς
ὅτι τοῖς ἁμαρτωλοῖς συγκατεδικάσθη καὶ συγκεκρέμαται δι' ἡμᾶς ὁ μὴ εἰδὼς ἁμαρτίαν
ἵνα ἡμεῖς γενώμεθα δικαιοσύνη Θεοῦ ἐν αὐτῷ· δεδικαιώμεθα γὰρ παρὰ τοῦ Θεοῦ καὶ
Πατρὸς "οὐκ ἐξ ἔργων τῶν ἐν δικαιοσύνῃ ὧν ἐποιήσαμεν "ἡμεῖς, ἀλλὰ κατὰ τὸ πολὺ
αὐτοῦ ἔλεος" διὰ πίστεως τῆς ἐν Χριστῷ. Αὐτὸς δὲ ἐγὼ Παῦλος παρακαλῶ ὑμᾶς διὰ τῆς
πραότητος καὶ ἐπιεικείας τοῦ Χριστοῦ κ.τ.λ.
Πολλοὶ ἦσαν τῶν Ἀθήνῃσι σοφῶν, τοῖς ἐν Κορίνθῳ συνδιαιτώμενοι, οἳ μωρίαν
ἡγοῦντο τὸν τοῦ Σωτῆρος σταυρὸν, καὶ τὸν τῆς θεοπνεύστου γραφῆς διαγγέλλοντα
λόγον, ἀγύρτην καὶ σπερμολόγον ὁμοῦ τοῖς ἄλλοις ἁγίοις καὶ αὐτὸν ὠνόμαζον τὸν
μακάριον Παῦλον· ἕτεροι δέ τινες τῶν ἐκ περιτομῆς κατεπεφύοντο πάλιν τῶν
πεπιστευκότων, ἐπαινοῦντες τὴν περιτομὴν καὶ τὰς νομικὰς θυσίας, ἐξεστηκότα τε
λέγοντες τὸν μακάριον Παῦλον, ὡς τοῖς ἀρχαίοις θεσπίσμασιν ἀνοσίως πολεμεῖν
ᾑρημένον. πρὸς δὲ τοὺς τοιούτους παρωτρύνοντο μὲν καὶ μάλα εἰκότως τῶν Κορινθίων
οἱ ζηλωταὶ, χεῖρας δὲ αὐτοῖς ἐπιφέρειν ἤθελον, ὡς ἐχθροῖς τοῦ θείου κηρύγματος·
ἐπειδὴ δὲ ἦν ἀκαλλὲς λίαν τὸ χρῆμα, καὶ τῆς ἁγίοις πρεπούσης ἐπιεικείας ὡς ἀπωτάτω·
"∆οῦλον γὰρ "Κυρίου οὐ δεῖ μάχεσθαι, κατὰ τὸ γεγραμμένον, ἀλλ' ἤπιον 357 "εἶναι πρὸς
πάντας, ἐν πραότητι παιδεύοντα τοὺς ἀντιδια"τιθεμένους·" ἐπιτάττει λέγων Αὐτὸς δὲ
ἐγὼ Παῦλος ὁ τῶν θείων μυστηρίων ἱερουργὸς, ὁ ταμίας καὶ ἀπόστολος, ὁ ζήλῳ
διαπρεπὴς, παραθήγων καὶ ὑμᾶς αὐτοὺς εἰς τὸ λέγειν σὺν ἐμοί "̓Εμοὶ γὰρ τὸ ζῆν Χριστὸς
καὶ τὸ ἀποθανεῖν κέρδος," παρακαλῶ ὑμᾶς διὰ τῆς πραότητος καὶ ἐπιεικείας τοῦ
Χριστοῦ, "ὃς λοιδορούμενος οὐκ ἀντελοιδόρει, πάσχων οὐκ ἠπείλει, "παρεδίδου δὲ τῷ
κρίνοντι δικαίως." ἐπὶ καιροῦ τοιγαροῦν τῆς Χριστοῦ ζωῆς εἰς ἀνάμνησιν αὐτοὺς
ἀποφέρει, πραοτάτους καὶ ἐπιεικεῖς καθιστάς· ἐγὼ δὲ αὐτός φησιν Παῦλος ὁ παρὼν μὲν
ἐν ὑμῖν κατὰ πρόσωπόν εἰμι ταπεινὸς, οὐ γαῦρος, οὔτε μὴν ἠκονημένος εἰς ἔριδάς τε καὶ
μάχας, ὃς θαῤῥῶ μὲν ἀπὼν, δέομαι δὲ καὶ νῦν μὴ παρὼν θαῤῥῆσαι· ὅτι καθάπερ ἔπεισί
μοι λογίζεσθαι, κατ' οὐδένα τρόπον τολμήσετε κατά τινων οἰομένων ἡμᾶς ὡς κατὰ
σάρκα περιπατεῖν, τουτέστι πολιτεύεσθαι σαρκικῶς ἐν ἔριδί τε καὶ ζήλῳ· "ὅπου γὰρ,
φησὶ, "ζῆλος καὶ ἔρις ἐν ὑμῖν, οὐχὶ σαρκικοί ἐστε καὶ κατὰ ἄν"θρωπον περιπατεῖτε;"
κρείττους οὖν ἄρα τῆς ἐκείνων ὑποψίας γενέσθαι προσήκει τοὺς ἀκολουθεῖν ἐθέλοντας

15

ταῖς τοῦ Σωτῆρος ἐπιεικείαις, καὶ μὴ σαρκικῶς περιπατεῖν. εἰ γὰρ ἀπειθοῦσί τινες, οὐ
ξύλοις αὐτοὺς καταπαίοντας καταβιάζεσθαι χρὴ, περιμένειν δὲ μᾶλλον τὴν ἑκούσιον

review_notes: Opens mid-sentence: ἀναπίπτειν εἰς ῥᾳθυμίας completes the last clause of u04-rem-early (…καὶ πρὸς τὸ ἀναπεῖσαι ῥᾳδίως μὴ | ἀναπίπτειν, 'to persuade them easily not to fall back'). Marked with a leading ellipsis; no words supplied.
Ends mid-sentence at περιμένειν δὲ μᾶλλον τὴν ἑκούσιον; u04-rem-close opens with αὐτῶν πρὸς Θεὸν ἐπιστροφήν ('their turning to God'). The paragraph ends with an ellipsis.

Negation and agency kept exact: the Father is the subject of 'made sin' (περὶ τοῦ Θεοῦ καὶ Πατρός); μὴ ὑπολάβῃς ὅτι πέπραχεν ἁμαρτίαν, 'do not suppose that He committed sin'; οὐ γὰρ οἶδεν πλημμελεῖν, 'does not know how to do wrong'; δέομαι … μὴ παρὼν θαῤῥῆσαι, 'that when present I may not have to be bold'; οὐ ξύλοις … καταβιάζεσθαι χρή, 'one must not … force them'.

ἁμαρτίας ὠνόμαζον: the sin-offering victims were called 'sins' (LXX usage of ἁμαρτία for the sin offering, e.g. Leviticus 4:24, 4:25); possible allusion, not cited inline. The priests' eating of the sin offering echoes Leviticus 6:26 (LXX 6:19); possible, not cited inline.

συγκεκρέμαται: 'hung beside them', the crucifixion between criminals (compare Luke 23:32–33; Isaiah 53:12); possible allusion, not cited inline. δέδοται … ὑπὲρ τῶν ἁμαρτιῶν ἡμῶν may echo Galatians 1:4; possible, not cited inline.

ὁ ταμίας: 'steward' (compare 1 Corinthians 4:1, οἰκονόμους μυστηρίων θεοῦ); possible allusion, not cited inline. ἐξεστηκότα may echo 2 Corinthians 5:13 (εἴτε γὰρ ἐξέστημεν); possible, not cited inline.
κατεπεφύοντο: 'were setting upon' (καταφύομαι, to fasten on, attack).
The Corinthian zealots' wish to use force is Cyril's reconstruction of the setting; it is rendered as he gives it, without softening.
Page markers 356, 357 and the page number 15 are omitted.
Divine pronouns are capitalised for clarity, which also keeps the Father ('He made') distinct from Christ ('Him who knew no sin') and from Paul ('he says').

Review: Staged row reviewed against the Greek: faithful, citations correct (2 Corinthians 5:21, 5:14, Hebrews 12:2, Hosea 4:8 LXX, Titus 3:5, 2 Corinthians 10:1–2, 1 Corinthians 1:23, 3:3, Acts 17:18, 2 Timothy 2:24–25, Philippians 1:21, 1 Peter 2:23). Fixed in place in tr0.json for word order only: 'the One who had never sinned at all, He caused to suffer...' -> 'He caused the One who had never sinned at all to suffer...'; 'the One who was worth as much as all' -> 'He whose worth equals that of all'; reordered the 'charlatan and babbler' sentence; 'as it comes to my mind to reckon ... venture against' -> 'as I am minded to think ... take bold action against' (τολμήσετε echoes 10:2 θαρρῆσαι/τολμῆσαι). Joins cleanly with u04-rem-early ('not to …') and u04-rem-close ('… turning to God').
